title: Lichtman Predicts Democrats Will Take Both Chambers In Midterms
excerpt: The historian who correctly called nine of the past 11 presidential races forecasts a Democratic House and Senate — a prediction, made on Election Day, that voters will now test.
body:
• Historian Allan Lichtman predicts Democrats will win both the House and the Senate in the November 3 midterms — a forecast made as voting takes place, not a result.
  • He puts the chance of a Democratic House win above 90% and a Senate win at 67%, with a 51-49 Senate majority as his most likely outcome.
  • His famous 13 Keys system was built for presidential races; this midterm call uses a different method, and he says he has no formal midterm model.
  • For voters heading out today: control of Congress will decide confirmations, investigations and how much of President Donald Trump's agenda can move — confirm your polling place and ballot status before you go.

Allan Lichtman, the American University historian often called the "Nostradamus" of U.S. elections, has predicted that Democrats will take control of both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections, a result that would strip President Donald Trump's Republican Party of its majorities. The call, set out in interviews with The Times and USA TODAY, is a prediction, not an outcome, and it will be tested as results come in.

The forecast: House above 90%, Senate at 67%

Lichtman puts Democrats' chances of winning the House at more than 90%. Republicans currently hold a narrow 218-214 majority, so Democrats need only a handful of seats to take control. "Democrats need so few seats to take the majority. I give it over a 90% chance," he told The Times, in remarks reported by UNILAD on November 3. He told USA TODAY it is "almost certain that Democrats will take back the House of Representatives."

The Senate is a harder climb. Republicans hold a 53-47 advantage, meaning Democrats need a net gain of four seats. Lichtman puts their chances at 67% — about two-thirds — with a 51-49 Democratic majority as his most likely outcome. His final assessment has Democrats gaining seats in Maine, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas while holding Michigan. He has also pointed to Democratic competitiveness in states Republicans usually win comfortably, saying: "It's amazing that Democrats are competitive in South Carolina, which Trump won by 18 points."

How he made the call

Lichtman's reputation rests on his 13 Keys system for presidential elections, through which he correctly predicted nine of the past 11 races — the winners in 1984, 1988, 1992, 1996, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016 and 2020, according to USA TODAY. He missed in 2000, when he predicted Al Gore over George W. Bush, and in 2024, when he predicted Kamala Harris would defeat Trump.

This midterm forecast does not use the 13 Keys. "To the best of my recollection, never in this depth with this specificity. I do not have a formal model for midterm elections," he told USA TODAY. Instead, he weighed four factors: historical patterns that weigh against the party holding the White House, generic congressional polls favouring Democrats, voter enthusiasm, and Democratic wins in 2025 off-year and special elections. He said Democrats lead Republicans by seven to 11 points in the generic congressional ballot, which he treats as a more reliable guide than individual race polls, and that Democratic enthusiasm is higher this cycle, reversing the usual Republican turnout edge.

"When the approval rating for a president is as low as Trump's, on average the White House party loses 40 House and six Senate seats. It's not a prediction, that's just showing how heavily the winds are blowing against Republicans."

Lichtman stressed that the 40 House and six Senate seat figures are historical averages for presidents with approval ratings as low as Trump's, not his prediction. On average, he noted, the White House party loses about 25 House seats and three Senate seats in a midterm, and only three times since the Civil War has it gained House seats. Other forecasters broadly agree on the House; the Cook Political Report moved from calling the Senate a toss-up on September 23 to saying on October 6 that the majority was "squarely in Democrats' sights," USA TODAY reported.

What a flip would mean

Lichtman told USA TODAY that Senate control is "so critical [for Democrats] because the Senate passes on appointees, cabinet members, military leaders and lifetime judges, and so control of the Senate means control over Trump appointees." A Democratic Congress could also open investigations and slow the administration's legislative agenda, while Lichtman has acknowledged his own record is fallible. "Look, I've been doing this for over 40 years. No forecaster ever in the history of the world, including the great Nostradamus, is perfect," he said. Voters will deliver the verdict today.
